(a) Availability of Funds.—
        (1) In general.— Of the funds authorized to be appropriated by this Act or otherwise made available for fiscal year 2014 for research, development, test, and evaluation, Defense-wide, for the Missile Defense Agency, not more than $15,000,000 may be obligated or expended for nonrecurring engineering costs in connection with the establishment of a capacity for co-production in the United States by industry of the United States of parts and components for the Iron Dome short-range rocket defense program. Such obligation or expenditure shall be made pursuant to an agreement described in paragraph (2). 
        (2) Agreement described.—An agreement described in this paragraph is an agreement entered into by the Government of the United States and the Government of Israel with respect to the co-production in the United States of parts and components for the Iron Dome short-range rocket defense program.  
    (b) Report on Co-production.—Not later than 30 days after obligating or expending funds specified in subsection (a), the 
Director of the Missile Defense Agency shall submit to the congressional defense committees a report on the plan to implement an agreement described in paragraph (2) of such subsection, including the following:
        (1) A description of the estimated cost of implementing the agreement, including the costs to be paid by industry. 
        (2) The expected schedule to implement the agreement. 
        (3) A description of any efforts to minimize the costs of the agreement to the Government of the United States.  
    (c) Report on Missile Defense Cooperation.—
        (1) In general.—Not later than one year after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the congressional defense committees a report on the status of missile defense cooperation between the United States and Israel. 
        (2) Elements.—The report under paragraph (1) shall include the following:
            (A) A description of the current program of ballistic missile defense cooperation between the United States and Israel, including the objectives and results of such cooperation as of the date of the report. 
            (B) A description of steps taken during the year prior to the report, and steps planned to be taken during the year following the report, by the governments of the United States and Israel to improve the coordination, interoperability, and integration of the missile defense capabilities of the United States and Israel. 
            (C) A description of joint missile defense exercises and training that have been conducted by the United States and Israel, and the lessons learned from such exercises. 
            (D) A description of joint efforts of the United States and Israel to develop ballistic missile defense technologies and capabilities. 
            (E) Any other matters that the Secretary considers appropriate.   
    (d) Construction.—Nothing in this section shall be construed to alter or affect the procurement schedule, or anticipated procurement numbers, under the Iron Dome short-range rocket defense program. 
    (e) Sense of Congress.—It is the sense of Congress that—
        (1) second-source production of parts and components of the Iron Dome short-range rocket defense program that is based in the United States is in the national security interest of both Israel and the United States; and 
        (2) the move towards such a second-source capacity in the United States for integration and assembly of all-up rounds of the Iron Dome short-range rocket defense program will further enhance the security of Israel by ensuring added production capability of such vital program.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the U.S.-Israel co-production agreement and the references to industry bring outside parties into a federal decision. But the agreement is only a funding precondition set by an international government-to-government arrangement, not a consultation, comment, hearing, or advisory process on a federal decision. The section's only procedural requirements are reports to the congressional defense committees, which stay inside the federal government. Nothing grants any outside party a right to be consulted, to object, or to sue.
fable.s: the Director of the Missile Defense Agency shall submit to the congressional defense committees a report on the plan to implement an agreement described in paragraph (2) of such subsection

qwen_block.w: The section primarily authorizes funding for an agreement between the US and Israel and requires reports to be submitted to congressional defense committees. Congress is part of the federal government, so reporting to it is internal government communication, not participation by outside parties. The agreement with Israel is an executive action, and the text does not mandate consultation with non-federal entities (like the public, states, or independent experts) before making decisions; it merely describes the agreement's existence and requires reporting on it.
qwen_block.s: the Director of the Missile Defense Agency shall submit to the congressional defense committees a report on the plan to implement an agreement described in paragraph (2) of such subsection

opus.w: Spending the money depends on an agreement between the U.S. and Israeli governments. That is a diplomatic deal between two governments, not a process like a comment period, hearing, advisory body or right to sue. The other procedural parts are reports to the congressional defense committees, and Congress is inside the federal government. The tempting Yes reading treats Israel as an outside participant, but negotiating an agreement with another country is not participation in the sense the definition describes.

opus.b:
I'm labelling this **No**, with moderate confidence (0.65).

1. **The tempting reading.** The money can only be spent "pursuant to an agreement" between the U.S. and Israeli governments. Israel's government is outside the U.S. federal government, so this could look like an outside party taking part in a federal decision.

2. **Why it doesn't fit.** The Israel agreement is a deal between two governments about co-producing parts, made through diplomacy. It is not an outside party being consulted or given a say through a comment period, hearing, advisory panel, or right to sue. Treaty-style deals between sovereign governments don't fit the kind of participation the definition describes.

3. **The rest of the section.** Subsections (b) and (c) only require reports to the congressional defense committees, and Congress is inside the federal government. The "costs to be paid by industry" and the Sense of Congress don't give anyone outside the government a role in the decision either.

The confidence is moderate because a literal reading of the "single gate" could treat a foreign government as an outside party and answer Yes.

qwen_chat.w: The section mandates reports to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government, and thus does not constitute participation. The agreement with Israel is an executive action regarding co-production, not a statutory requirement for public consultation or advisory input. There is no requirement for the federal government to consult with outside parties (public, states, experts) before making a decision.
qwen_chat.s: Not later than 30 days after obligating or expending funds specified in subsection (a), the Director of the Missile Defense Agency shall submit to the congressional defense committees a report on the plan to implement an agreement described in paragraph (2) of such subsection
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the "agreement" between the US and Israel involves coordination with an outside entity (Israel), or that the reports to Congress involve participation. However, reports to Congress are explicitly excluded because Congress is inside the federal government. The agreement with Israel is a bilateral executive agreement regarding procurement/co-production, not a statutory requirement for public consultation or advisory input into a domestic regulatory decision. The section primarily authorizes spending and mandates internal reporting. There is no requirement for the federal government to consult with the public, states, tribes, or independent experts before making a decision. The "industry of the United States" is mentioned as the producer, but the text does not require consultation with them; it just authorizes funds for their work.
